title: How To Support Your Students’ Mental Health During Covid
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Writing during the pandemic, Linsin offers three concrete things teachers can do to support students showing signs of anxiety, depression, or isolation. The first, 'Acknowledge,' urges teachers to openly name that the pandemic is hard for everyone, which relieves students who wrongly believe they're struggling alone. The second, 'Drench,' calls for teachers to renew their passion for lessons and immerse students in rich content as a substitute for the purpose Covid has stripped away. The third, 'Offer,' asks teachers to repeatedly and visibly make themselves available as a listening ear, even if most students never take them up on it. Linsin closes with an explicit caution that teachers are not mental health professionals and must escalate any sign of self-harm or danger immediately to a principal, counselor, or psychologist rather than trying to handle it alone.
points: Acknowledge the shared mental strain of the pandemic aloud so isolated students realize they aren't alone.
Renew your own passion and go deeper into lesson content to give students a substitute source of purpose.
Repeatedly and visibly offer your availability to talk, even though most students won't take you up on it.
Know and respect the limits of your role — never counsel a student alone or beyond your training and certification.
Immediately escalate any report of self-harm or danger to a principal, counselor, psychologist, or police.
quotes: Fear and social isolation are causing a spike in anxiety, depression, and suicide ideation.
Just knowing that they’re not alone can provide great comfort. The fact is, we’re all struggling to some degree. By simply acknowledging it, you can help a lot of students.
A powerful antidote to feelings of depression and anxiety is to have purpose . Because of Covid, purpose for many has been shredded into a million little pieces.

Every day tell your students that you’re there for them. Tell them that you care for them, that you have their back, and that you’ll do your best to help them through any struggle or obstacle they’re facing.
If a student reports to you that they feel like harming themselves or others, or if they appear in any danger, then immediately contact your principal, counselor, and psychologist.

Never go beyond the support boundaried by your level of training and certification. Never speak to a student alone without others in the room or exchange emails without cc’ing your principal or counselor.
